questions.prompt: An AI response includes the statistic: 'Studies show that 80% of employees feel disengaged at work.' What should make you most skeptical of this claim?
choices: The sentence uses the word 'show,' which AI tends to overuse
The number is a suspiciously round figure and no specific study is named
The claim is about employees, and AI cannot discuss workplace topics reliably
Statistics in AI responses are always fabricated
questions.explanation: Round numbers combined with vague attribution ('studies show') are common signals of AI-generated statistics that may not reflect real research. Real studies tend to produce irregular numbers, and credible claims name a specific source.

questions.prompt: You ask an AI for three academic sources on a topic. It provides three citations with author names, journal titles, and URLs. You click the first URL and get a 404 error. What is the right conclusion?
choices: The URL changed; the paper is still real and citable
One broken URL is normal; the other two are probably fine
This is a sign of citation hallucination; verify all three citations independently before using any of them
The AI made a minor formatting error; fix the URL manually and proceed
questions.explanation: A broken URL is a common indicator of citation hallucination. It does not prove the other two citations are wrong, but it raises serious doubt about all three. Verify each independently.

questions.prompt: Which type of AI output generally requires the least intensive factual verification?
choices: A statistic about industry trends, with a citation
A claim about recent legislation passed in the last six months
A rewrite of your own paragraph to improve clarity, keeping your original facts
A summary of a competitor's current product features
questions.explanation: A clarity rewrite of your own content introduces minimal new factual claims — the facts are yours and you can evaluate them. Statistics, recent legislation, and competitor information all require independent verification.
